strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem in V2A generation: physical grounding of generated sounds with respect to object mass and velocity, rather than purely appearance-driven audio-visual correlation.

The proposed pipeline (PPE + Phy-Adapter) is reasonably well-engineered, combining VLM-based mass estimation, open-vocabulary segmentation, and dynamic 3D reconstruction for metric-scale velocity, and integrates physics cues via a residual delta-modulation mechanism that is shown to outperform naive summation in ablations.

New benchmark (VGG-Impact) and new metric (APCC) are useful contributions toward more rigorous evaluation of physical plausibility in V2A, addressing a real gap in existing perceptual/semantic metrics.

Quantitative results across a wide range of baselines (9 models) show consistent improvements on both perceptual metrics (FD, KL, IS, IB-score, DeSync) and the proposed APCC-Delta metric, and the ablation study isolates the contribution of mass vs. velocity conditioning and modulation strategy.
A user study with physical plausibility ratings supports the quantitative claims and shows PAVAS is rated favorably compared to baselines on multiple perceptual axes.
weaknesses: The accuracy of the core physics estimators (mass from VLM, velocity from monocular dynamic 3D reconstruction) is only briefly asserted ("comparable to, or even surpassing, specialized expert models") with details deferred entirely to supplementary material not included here; without seeing this validation in the main paper, the central premise that these physics estimates are reliable enough to condition generation is not verifiable from the manuscript body alone.

Monocular metric-scale velocity/mass estimation from single video, especially via VLM text-based reasoning, is inherently noisy and possibly scene/camera-scale ambiguous; no uncertainty quantification or failure-case analysis is presented in the main text to characterize how estimation errors propagate to audio quality.

The APCC metric itself depends on the same imperfect PPE-derived physical quantities (kinetic energy from estimated mass/velocity) to evaluate physical consistency, creating a potential circularity: a model conditioned on PPE outputs may naturally correlate better with PPE-derived ground truth than models that never see such signals, which could bias the benchmark in favor of the proposed method.

VGG-Impact benchmark is relatively small (272 impact moments, 10 classes) and manually curated by the authors, raising questions about selection bias and statistical robustness of the reported APCC differences; no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany Table 1.

Backbone parameter/architecture comparisons are somewhat uneven (only Large variants of MMAudio and PAVAS run at 44.1kHz while baselines run at 16kHz), which could confound perceptual quality metrics like FD/IS beyond the physics-conditioning contribution.

The user study is modest in scale (15 participants, 8 audio samples) which limits the statistical power of the subjective evaluation, and no significance testing is reported for the differences in Table 2.

The system relies on several large pretrained modules (VLM, Grounded-SAM2, CUT3R) chained together, and the paper does not report runtime/inference cost overhead relative to baselines, which is relevant for practical usefulness given the added complexity for a modest quantitative gain over MMAudio-L in several metrics (e.g., FD_VGG, KL_PANNs where MMAudio is comparable or better).

strengths: Addresses an interesting and underexplored problem: moving V2A generation beyond appearance-only correlations toward explicit physical grounding (mass, velocity).

The overall system design (PPE + Phy-Adapter with FiLM modulation and zero-initialized residual Δ-modulation injected via AdaLN) is a reasonable and relatively lightweight engineering contribution that is compatible with existing multimodal DiT backbones.

The paper proposes a new benchmark (VGG-Impact) and a new metric (APCC) targeting physical consistency, which, if validated, could be a useful contribution to the community beyond this specific method.

Extensive comparisons against many recent V2A baselines (See&Hear, V-AURA, VATT, Frieren, FoleyCrafter, V2A-Mapper, TARO, MMAudio) on standard metrics (FD, KL, IS, IB-score, DeSync), plus a user study and ablations, giving a reasonably broad empirical picture.
Qualitative spectrogram comparisons are illustrative and support the claim that the model better captures transient/impact dynamics in a couple of showcased examples.
weaknesses: The core physical grounding claim rests on VLM-based mass estimation from a single video, which is not actually measuring physics from visual dynamics but is largely a category-level semantic prior (e.g., "hammers weigh ~X kg"); no quantitative validation of mass-estimation accuracy against ground-truth measured masses is shown in the main paper, and the "comparable to or surpassing specialized expert models" claim is asserted without any table or number in the main text, only deferred to supplementary.

Monocular, unconstrained-video metric-scale 3D reconstruction (CUT3R) is known to be unreliable for absolute scale without camera calibration or known object priors; the paper does not discuss or quantify the scale/metric accuracy of the recovered velocities, which undermines confidence in the velocity estimator that feeds the whole pipeline.

The APCC metric and the VGG-Impact ground-truth "kinetic energy" signal are themselves derived from the same class of VLM/3D-reconstruction estimators used for conditioning, raising a risk of circularity: the model may simply be learning to exploit idiosyncrasies of the estimator's outputs rather than genuine physical realism, and this concern is not addressed (e.g., no comparison against independently measured/annotated physical ground truth).

No ablation isolates the effect of estimation quality (e.g., conditioning on oracle/ground-truth mass-velocity vs. estimated values) to determine whether gains stem from accurate physical reasoning or merely from additional object-centric/motion-aware conditioning signals, which could improve scores for reasons unrelated to "physics."

VGG-Impact is small (272 clips, 10 classes) and curated via unspecified manual filtering criteria without reported inter-annotator agreement, limiting confidence in its representativeness and reproducibility.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix models operating at different audio sample rates (16kHz baselines vs. 44.1kHz PAVAS/MMAudio-L), which, despite being noted, complicates strictly fair perceptual/distributional comparisons for most of the baseline set.

The user study is based on only 15 participants rating a small set of generated samples, which is a fairly limited sample for subjective claims about "physical plausibility," a notion that is also not well defined for lay raters.

Ablation gains attributable to the Δ-modulation design versus direct summation are numerically modest (e.g., FD_PaSST 67.31 vs 65.67, IS 16.30 vs 16.50), raising questions about how much of the overall improvement is specifically due to the proposed injection mechanism versus the addition of any extra conditioning pathway.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem in V2A generation: appearance-driven models often ignore whether the *magnitude* of generated sound (loudness, spectral sharpness) reflects underlying physical dynamics such as impact energy, and the paper motivates this gap clearly with a concrete example (Fig. 1).

The proposed Physics Parameter Estimator is a reasonable engineering solution to estimating object mass (via VLM prompting) and metric-scale velocity (via open-vocabulary segmentation + dynamic 3D reconstruction) from monocular, unconstrained video without requiring calibrated multi-view input, unlike prior geometry-based approaches (e.g., NeRF2Physics).

The Phy-Adapter's residual Δ-modulation design is well-motivated and empirically validated: the ablation (Table 3C) shows it outperforms naive summation, and injecting physics features gradually via zero-initialized gates is a sensible way to preserve the stability of a pretrained multimodal backbone while adding new conditioning signals.

The new VGG-Impact benchmark and APCC metric fill a real gap, since existing V2A benchmarks (VGGSound) evaluate only perceptual/semantic alignment, not physical consistency between kinetic energy and acoustic onset strength.

Strong, consistent empirical improvements: PAVAS outperforms nine competitive V2A baselines (including the strong MMAudio-L) across essentially all reported metrics—distributional (FD, KL), perceptual (IS), semantic (IB-score), temporal (DeSync), and the new physics metric (APCC)—as well as in a 15-participant user study across four subjective dimensions.

Reasonably thorough ablations isolate the contribution of mass-only, velocity-only, and combined conditioning, and compare against simply training the backbone longer, helping to rule out the possibility that gains are merely from extra optimization rather than the physics-aware components.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation circularity: APCC is computed using the same class of estimated physical quantities (VLM-based mass, CUT3R-based velocity) that PAVAS is explicitly conditioned on during generation. Since PAVAS is trained to reproduce sounds correlated with exactly these estimated physics values, its superior APCC score may partly reflect this shared estimation pipeline rather than a more fundamental notion of physical realism; a metric or validation less tied to the model's own conditioning signals (e.g., against independently measured ground-truth physical quantities) would strengthen the claim.

The main text does not report the quantitative accuracy of the mass and velocity estimators against ground truth (deferred entirely to supplementary material), yet the claim that PPE is 'comparable to or surpassing' specialized expert models is stated as a headline finding in the introduction; without seeing this evidence in the main paper, this claim cannot be fully assessed.

VGG-Impact is small in scale (272 impact moments across 10 classes), and while the paper describes a careful manual filtering process, the benchmark's diversity and statistical robustness (e.g., variance across classes, inter-annotator agreement in curation) are not discussed, limiting confidence in the generalizability of APCC results.

The physical model is limited to a single time-invariant scalar mass and per-frame centroid velocity per object; it does not model material/elasticity/restitution properties that also strongly shape impact sound (e.g., a rubber ball vs. a metal ball of the same mass and velocity would sound very different), so the notion of 'physical realism' captured here is a partial one, worth acknowledging more explicitly as a scope limitation.

No analysis of computational overhead or failure modes: the pipeline chains several large pretrained models (VLM, Florence-2, SAM2, CUT3R) purely for physics estimation at inference time, but runtime cost, estimator failure/error cases (e.g., VLM mass hallucination for unfamiliar objects, 3D reconstruction failures under fast motion or occlusion), and their downstream impact on generation quality are not analyzed in the main text.

Fairness of the baseline comparison in Table 1 is slightly muddied by the fact that most baselines run at 16kHz while PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L run at 44.1kHz; although this mirrors standard practice from prior work, it means the largest, most direct comparison is effectively only against MMAudio-L, with other baselines at a structural disadvantage for distributional metrics.

Aggregation of per-object modulated features via gated pooling (Eq. 9) collapses multiple simultaneous objects/impacts into a single conditioning vector per frame, which could blur fine-grained timing when multiple impact events with different mass/velocity occur close together in time; the paper does not discuss how well this handles multi-object interaction scenes.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap in V2A generation: existing models are appearance-driven and ignore explicit physical dynamics (mass, velocity) that shape real-world sound.

Proposes a full, well-engineered pipeline (PPE + Phy-Adapter with FiLM modulation and a delta-modulation residual injection mechanism) that is compatible with a modern multimodal diffusion transformer backbone, and shows via ablation that each physics stream (mass, velocity) and the residual injection strategy contribute measurable gains over a longer-trained backbone baseline.

Introduces a new benchmark (VGG-Impact) and a new interpretable metric (APCC) targeting physical plausibility, which is a genuine methodological contribution beyond standard perceptual/semantic V2A metrics.

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparison against 8 strong baselines, a 27-participant user study with consistent gains including on the newly introduced physical-plausibility dimension, and substantial supplementary analyses (mass/velocity estimator validation against expert baselines, sensitivity/robustness to perturbed or missing physics cues, runtime profiling, generalization beyond impact-centric scenes).

Reasonable design choices for open-world generalization (VLM-based mass reasoning, open-vocabulary segmentation + dynamic 3D reconstruction for metric-scale velocity) rather than requiring calibrated multi-view setups as in prior mass-estimation work.

Qualitative spectrogram comparisons and supplementary video convincingly illustrate cases (goad honking, golf driving, dog barking, wood chopping) where PAVAS avoids duplicated/misaligned/overextended acoustic events compared to baselines.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation bias in APCC: the same PPE used to condition PAVAS is also used to derive the reference kinetic-energy signal for the metric, meaning PAVAS is directly optimized toward correlating with the exact signal used for its own evaluation, which could inflate its advantage over baselines independent of true physical realism; a more independent physics ground truth (e.g., sensor-based or simulation-based) would strengthen the claim.

The physical model used is quite coarse: a single time-invariant scalar mass plus centroid-based translational velocity ignores material stiffness/elasticity, contact geometry, rotational motion, and resonance properties that strongly determine real impact sounds, so the 'physics-aware' claim is somewhat narrower than the framing suggests (acknowledged as future work but still a substantive limitation).
VGG-Impact benchmark is relatively small after filtering (272 impact moments across 10 classes), limiting the statistical robustness of the APCC-based comparisons.

Mass and velocity estimator validations rely on proxy benchmarks (ABO-500 for static multi-view objects, STARSS23 with a pseudo-ground-truth pipeline for velocity) that may not fully represent the dynamic, in-the-wild VGGSound/VGG-Impact conditions where PAVAS is actually deployed, so estimator reliability in the target domain is not directly verified against real ground truth.

Gains on some standard distributional/perceptual metrics over the strongest baseline (MMAudio-L) are modest or mixed (e.g., FD_VGG and KL_PANNs are comparable or slightly worse), so improvements are concentrated in physics-consistency measures rather than uniformly across all axes.

The pipeline depends on multiple heavy pretrained modules (VLM, Grounded-SAM2, CUT3R) with CUT3R dominating runtime, raising practical concerns about inference cost and scalability that are noted but not resolved.

Presentation is dense with many symbols/equations in the main text; some architectural details (e.g., precise interaction between object-centric features and multimodal condition) require cross-referencing the supplementary material to fully follow.

strengths: Addresses an interesting and under-explored problem: injecting explicit physical priors (mass, velocity) into V2A diffusion generation rather than relying purely on appearance-driven correlations.

Introduces a new benchmark (VGG-Impact) and a new evaluation metric (APCC) intended to measure physical consistency between kinetic energy and acoustic onset strength, which is a useful conceptual contribution even if imperfect.

Extensive experimental protocol: quantitative comparison against 8 baselines, a user study with a dedicated 'physical plausibility' axis, and thorough ablations (physics feature contribution, injection strategy, model scaling).

Substantial supplementary validation attempting to justify the reliability of the physics estimators (mass on ABO-500, velocity on STARSS23) and robustness analyses (perturbation sensitivity, graceful fallback with missing cues).

Reasonably engineered conditioning mechanism (Δ-modulation with zero-initialized residual gates) that is shown via ablation to outperform naive summation, and consistent, non-trivial gains over the strong MMAudio backbone across almost all reported metrics.
weaknesses: The physical grounding of the VLM-based mass estimator is questionable: outputs read like generic commonsense priors tied to object category/text (e.g., 'adult male ≈ 72kg', 'basketball ≈ 0.62kg') rather than measurements derived from actual visual evidence of the specific instance in the given video, raising doubts about whether the pipeline provides genuine 'physical reasoning' versus repackaged semantic/category priors already implicitly available to a V2A model conditioned on the same class label text.

The core evaluation metric APCC relies on a strong and unproven physical simplification — that spectral onset energy is proportional to kinetic energy lost at impact — ignoring material, geometry, damping, and radiation-efficiency factors that dominate real acoustic energy transfer; the only validation offered (class-shuffling, noise injection) shows the metric is sensitive to perturbation, not that it is a valid proxy for physical realism.

The velocity-estimation pipeline exhibits very high missing-observation rates in practice (65.15% of frames require SAM2/segmentation occlusion-token fallback per the supplementary statistics), which substantially undercuts the claim of reliable, densely available per-frame physical conditioning for in-the-wild video.

The PPE pipeline is heavy and computationally expensive (CUT3R alone costs ~4.8s per 10-second clip vs. 1.9s for the whole diffusion backbone), raising practicality concerns that are acknowledged but not meaningfully addressed.

Ablations validating the physics components (Table 3) are conducted only on the smallest S-16kHz variant, not on the main PAVAS-L model used for the headline comparisons, leaving open whether the same design choices and relative gains hold at the reported scale.

Mass is modeled as a single time-invariant scalar per detected object over an entire clip and is not disambiguated for object-object interactions (e.g., which of two colliding objects' mass actually governs the impact sound), which is conceptually under-specified for the paper's own target scenario of 'object-object interactions.'

The supplementary VGG-NonImpact comparison shows PAVAS-L still outperforming MMAudio-L on non-impact classes where physical mass/velocity conditioning should be largely irrelevant, suggesting a non-trivial portion of the reported gains may stem from generic architectural/training improvements (additional fine-tuning stage, extra parameters) rather than specifically from physics-awareness, which is not adequately disentangled.
The human evaluation is relatively small in scale (27 participants, only 8 clips), limiting the statistical robustness of the physical-plausibility and other subjective claims.

Mass/velocity estimator validation is performed on proxy, out-of-domain datasets (ABO-500 static product catalog images for mass; STARSS23 for velocity) rather than directly on the VGG-Impact test videos themselves, leaving the in-domain reliability of the estimated conditioning signals unverified where it matters most.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: most V2A work is appearance-driven, and this paper explicitly targets physical grounding (mass, velocity) as a conditioning signal, which is a meaningful conceptual contribution to the field.

The proposed VGG-Impact benchmark and APCC metric fill a real evaluation gap; prior benchmarks (e.g., VGGSound) only assess semantic/perceptual alignment, not physical consistency, so these artifacts have standalone value for future research even beyond this specific method.

Comprehensive empirical validation: the paper does not just report end-to-end V2A numbers but also independently validates the mass estimator against NeRF2Physics/Image2mass on ABO-500 and the velocity estimator against a SpatialVLM-derived pseudo-ground-truth pipeline on STARSS23, which strengthens confidence that the physics cues being injected are meaningful rather than arbitrary.

Strong ablation and robustness analysis: separate ablations for mass-only/velocity-only/combined conditioning, direct summation vs. Δ-modulation, sensitivity to injected perturbation/noise in physics values, and graceful fallback via occlusion tokens all support the design choices with evidence rather than assertion.

Results are consistent across quantitative metrics (FD, KL, IS, ImageBind, DeSync), the newly proposed APCC-Δ, a user study (27 participants, 4 criteria), and qualitative spectrogram comparisons, giving converging multi-modal evidence for the claimed improvements.

The method improves not only physical plausibility (APCC-Δ) but also standard perceptual/semantic/sync metrics relative to a strong recent baseline (MMAudio), suggesting the physics conditioning is not merely a trade-off against generation quality.

Reasonable implementation/reproducibility detail is provided in the supplementary (prompts, hyperparameters, architecture diagrams, runtime profiling, module-wise costs), which aids reproducibility despite the pipeline's complexity.
weaknesses: The physics parameter estimator is largely a composition of existing off-the-shelf components (Qwen2.5-VL, Grounded-SAM2/Florence-2, SAM2, CUT3R); the core technical novelty is concentrated in the Phy-Adapter and Δ-modulation fusion mechanism, which is comparatively lightweight, so the overall contribution leans more toward system-level integration and benchmark curation than fundamentally new modeling technique.

Mass estimation relies on a VLM's semantic/common-sense priors about object categories (e.g., 'hammer ≈ X kg') rather than measurement from visual/physical evidence in the specific video; it is unclear how much of the reported 'physics awareness' is genuine visual physical reasoning versus retrieval of typical object masses from language priors, which could limit generalization to atypical objects (e.g., a hammer filled with lead vs. a toy hammer that look identical).

APCC evaluation and the physics conditioning both depend on the same PPE pipeline: kinetic energy targets used to score physical plausibility are derived from the same estimator used to condition the generator, raising a potential circularity/self-consistency concern that is only partially addressed by the noise-injection and shuffling robustness checks in the supplementary.

VGG-Impact is quite small (272 impact moments across 10 classes) and derived from a single source dataset (VGGSound), limiting the breadth of physical interaction types (e.g., no clear coverage of material-varying elastic/inelastic collisions across categories) and raising questions about statistical robustness of APCC differences across methods.

Performance is not uniformly best across all metrics in Table 1 (e.g., FD_VGG and KL_PANNs are better for V2A-Mapper/VATT than PAVAS-L), which is appropriately reported but slightly undercuts the framing that physics conditioning uniformly improves generation quality.

The user study is modest in scale (27 participants, only 8 clips), which is standard for such studies but still limits the statistical power of the physical-plausibility subjective claims relative to the strength of the paper's rhetoric.

The method's mass is modeled as strictly time-invariant per object and velocity is limited to per-object centroid motion; more complex physical phenomena (rotational dynamics, material stiffness/elasticity, multi-object simultaneous contacts) are not modeled, which the paper acknowledges only briefly as future work rather than as a current limitation of scope.
